newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs get cold feet about energy saving laws.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs get cold feet about energy saving laws.

text.p: The European Parliament's energy committee (CERT) failed on Tuesday in its attempt to force EU member states by law to tackle energy saving more seriously.

When the parliament gave a second reading on Tuesday to a proposed five-year energy saving programme (SAVE II) for the European Union, it demanded a series of amendments designed to widen the scope of the scheme.

But to the disappointment of rapporteur Undine-Uta Bloch von Blottnitz (German Green), the majority of Euro-MPs rejected amendments from CERT which would have committed the EU and national governments to introducing new binding legislation to force through improvements in energy efficiency.

In CERT's view, unless new legislation gets on the statute books quickly, CO2 emissions in the EU will increase by five to eight percent between 1995 and 2000, at a time when the Union is committed to bringing emissions back down to 1990 levels before the turn of the century.

Bloch von Blottnitz's report on the SAVE II proposal -- (COM(95)225 -- points out that its predecessor, SAVE I, did little to bring about more efficient use of energy but that what it did achieve was primarily as a result of new EU laws.
The German Green said after the vote that parliament's refusal to support a hard-hitting new programme was shameful.

Presenting her report to the parliament on Monday evening, Bloch von Blottnitz slammed the Council for axing the planned SAVE II budget by over two thirds, bringing it down from 150 million Ecus to 45 million.

The EU depended on imports for 70 percent of its energy demand and the Council should be taking energy saving more seriously, she said, pointing out that ministers appeared quite happy to provide one billion Ecus to support the controviersial tobacco industry next year.
Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis admitted to Euro-MPs on Monday there had been little progress in boosting energy efficiency or cutting CO2 emissions.
He accepted the 45-million-Ecu budget was too small but said he hoped it could at least serve as a top-up to national programmes.
